question:
A senior risk analyst at a German Landesbank is presenting the history of derivatives capital rules to newly hired analysts. She drafts four statements about the treatment of netting before and after the 1995 Amendment to the 1988 Basel Accord:

I. Under the original 1988 Accord, a bank that hedged a swap by entering an offsetting swap with the same counterparty attracted an add-on on each swap, so hedging was discouraged.

II. The original 1988 Accord gave almost no credit for netting because the Basel Committee judged netting to be economically meaningless between counterparties that had signed a master agreement.

III. The 1995 Amendment allowed reductions in credit equivalent amounts only where enforceable bilateral netting agreements were in place.

IV. Equity and commodity derivatives, which the original 1988 Accord did not address, continued to fall outside the add-on framework after the 1995 Amendment.

Which of the statements are accurate?

Stem summary: German Landesbank analyst auditing four statements on netting before and after the 1995 Amendment.

Credit exposure on a derivative. When a bank holds an OTC derivative, it loses money on counterparty default only if the contract has a positive value to the bank at that moment (the bank is owed money). If the value is negative, the bank owes the counterparty and loses nothing from the default. On top of today’s value, the value can move before any default occurs, so Basel I added a “potential future exposure” add-on. Under the original 1988 Accord the credit equivalent amount of each contract was

CEA = max($V,$ 0) + $D \times L,$

Stem summary: Consultant validating the CEA for a UK counterparty whose four swaps exactly offset.

Why netting cannot remove the whole add-on. The add-on covers future movements. question: An internal auditor at a Brazilian commercial bank is preparing training material on how bank capital rules evolved before Basel II. Which of the following statements best describes the purpose and scope of the 1996 Amendment to the 1988 Basel Accord?

options.A: It added capital for the market risk of banking book positions, such as loans held for investment, because the 1988 credit risk rules did not capture that risk.
options.B: It added capital for the operational risk of trading book positions, because the 1987 stock market crash had exposed weaknesses in trading controls.
options.C: It replaced the 1988 credit risk charge with a market risk charge for all positions, because every asset held by a bank had to be marked to market.

Stem summary: Brazilian bank auditor choosing the statement that best describes the 1996 Amendment.

Two books, two risks. Banks hold positions for two purposes. The trading book holds bonds, marketable equities, commodities, foreign currencies and most derivatives held for trading; these are marked to market (fair value accounting), so their main risk is a change in market value.
